findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: The build executes whatever content is served by a mutable URL at build time. A compromised origin, DNS/proxy interception, or changed script can execute arbitrary code in the image build and produces non-reproducible artifacts.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer instead of piping it to sh
findings.whyItBreaks: Any party able to alter the response from this URL can execute arbitrary commands during image build. The URL is neither version-pinned nor protected by a checksum or signature, and the pipe hides the downloaded artifact from review.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build fetches and executes whatever this mutable URL serves. A compromised or changed endpoint compromises the build and resulting image, with no version pin or checksum verification.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in the public helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this helper discards it and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish an absent key from a present key whose legitimate value is empty, so they may treat missing configuration/data as valid.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key status instead of returning an empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: When the key is absent, Load returns "" and ErrMissing, but this line discards ErrMissing. Callers of the exported LoadOrDefault cannot distinguish an absent key from a present key mapped to "", so they can treat failed lookups as valid stored values.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in the public loader
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing and returns "", making an absent key indistinguishable from a present key whose value is intentionally empty. As an exported API, every caller is forced to conflate the failure with valid data.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each job is now sent by an untracked goroutine, so Run can return while sends are still pending. A caller that closes results after Run returns (safe under the previous synchronous implementation) can cause these goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also lose the guarantee that all jobs have been processed at return.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: The goroutines can still send after Run returns. A caller that closes its results channel once Run completes will cause a send-on-closed-channel panic; callers can also observe incomplete results at return time. Previously every send completed before return.

findings.title: Preserve completion before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Run now returns before any result is necessarily sent. A caller that closes results after Run returns (valid under the prior synchronous behavior) can cause the spawned senders to panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also no longer receive results in jobs order.

findings.title: Bound concurrent result senders
findings.whyItBreaks: The function creates one goroutine per job and returns immediately. If the receiver is slow or absent, every sender remains blocked at the channel send, so a large jobs slice creates an unbounded goroutine leak instead of the previous single blocked sender/backpressure behavior.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant ownership for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing && with || authorizes deletion when either condition alone is true. Any non-admin session can delete every record in its tenant, and an admin from tenant A can delete records in tenant B.

findings.title: Require admin status and tenant match for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Using OR authorizes an admin from tenant A to delete a record in tenant B, and also authorizes any non-admin tenant member to delete records. The prior conjunction required both privileges.

findings.title: Restore admin requirement for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: With `||`, a session where `isAdmin` is false but `tenantId` matches the record returns true. Any ordinary user in a tenant can therefore delete every record in that tenant, including records they do not own. The previous predicate required both admin status and tenant isolation.

findings.title: Preserve settings parse failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or incomplete settings now return valid-looking defaults instead of reporting the parse/validation failure. updateFontSize then changes that fallback and saves it, overwriting the original raw settings; previously the error prevented save from being called.

findings.title: Do not overwrite malformed settings with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid JSON or an invalid settings field now becomes a valid-looking default Settings object. updateFontSize then treats that fallback as real data and saves it, replacing a malformed-but-recoverable stored theme with "light" instead of preserving the previous behavior of surfacing the parse error and avoiding a write.

findings.title: Preserve invalid-settings errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts both JSON parse failures and explicit validation failures into valid-looking defaults. updateFontSize can no longer distinguish corrupt input from real settings and saves {"theme":"light","fontSize":size}, silently replacing the previous error path and losing the stored theme.

findings.title: Use the requested branch's artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom identifies the requested branch commit but artifacts are loaded from the verified commit. The report can therefore claim artifacts were built from one commit while returning another commit's artifacts; previously both fields used commit.

findings.title: Use the branch commit for report artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` remains the commit resolved from the requested `branch`, but `artifacts` are now fetched from the unrelated `verified` ref. Whenever those refs differ, the report falsely associates verified artifacts with the requested branch commit.

findings.title: Read artifacts from the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When build.ref(branch) and build.ref("verified") resolve to different commits, builtFrom reports the branch commit while artifacts are fetched from the verified commit. Consumers receive a self-contradictory BuildReport and can report or deploy artifacts from the wrong revision.

findings.title: Restore the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit. renderFeed passes 20 and then copies page.length entries, so feeds with more than 20 entries produce an output longer than its intended 20-entry page.

findings.title: Restore the limit cap in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns every entry instead of at most limit. renderFeed passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9, so input with more than 20 entries expands its preallocated output array and returns all entries rather than one page.

findings.title: Restore the limit when returning sorted entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every entry despite the documented "at most limit" contract. The in-repo caller passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9; when all has more than 20 entries, the loop at line 11 extends the preallocated array and renderFeed returns all entries rather than a 20-entry feed.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Stale entries are removed from rows, but the unchanged header still receives entries.length. For one live and one stale entry, the output declares '# entry-count: 2' while containing one entry row, making the serialized manifest internally inconsistent for consumers that use the header to validate or parse its contents.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry has stale=true, it is omitted from rows but headerLines still receives entries.length. For example, one live and one stale entry produces '# entry-count: 2' followed by one entry row, making the manifest's declared count incorrect.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Filtering stale entries removes their rows, but the unchanged header call still reports entries.length. A manifest with one live and one stale entry declares '# entry-count: 2' while containing one entry, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or parse the manifest.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting FormatLegacyID is a source-compatibility break: any external package importing ids and calling this exported function will no longer compile when upgrading.

findings.title: Retain FormatLegacyID as a supported exported API
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is exported, so downstream Go consumers can call it. Removing it makes those consumers fail to compile when updating, and removes the only implementation producing the documented-by-behavior LEG0000000042-style legacy identifier.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: The previously exported shippingQuote(order) API is removed. Existing consumers importing it from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading, despite quoteShipping preserving the calculation internally.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported function from this module before the change, but is now absent. Any consumer importing it from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading, even though quoteShipping provides equivalent calculation behavior in a different module.

findings.title: Return a string from execute
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return contract, but every invocation now throws before returning. Consumers that previously received the uppercase input instead receive an unhandled error.

findings.title: Return the declared string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute(input) is exported with a `string` return type, but every invocation now throws instead of returning the transformed input. Existing callers receive an exception where they previously received an uppercase string.

findings.title: Return a result instead of unconditionally throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute(input): string API now throws "always fails". The prior implementation returned the uppercased input, so all consumers lose the function's only successful behavior.

findings.title: Keep active viewers eligible for read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" at line 24, so the established "read-only" result at line 25 can never be returned.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now makes isEligible return false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24. Before this change, that same request reached line 25 and returned "read-only"; the viewer branch is now unreachable.

findings.title: Keep eligible viewers on the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: Active viewers below the attempt limit previously reached handle's viewer branch and returned "read-only". This new predicate rejects them first, so that branch is unreachable and valid read-only requests now return "rejected".

findings.title: Keep saving drafts independent of payment
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; a draft with `payment: "missing"` previously returns "saved" but now returns "blocked". Payment legitimately governs submission, not persisting a draft.

findings.title: Keep draft saving independent of payment status
findings.whyItBreaks: For { state: "draft", payment: "missing" }, canProceed now returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" at src/actions.ts:9. Previously the same valid draft returned "saved". Payment may govern submission, but it must not prevent a user from saving an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot declares commit=headCommit(channel), but files are read from headCommit("stable"). Whenever channel and stable differ, consumers receive files that do not belong to the reported commit or channel.

findings.title: Use the requested channel head for snapshot files
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot.commit identifies the requested channel commit but Snapshot.files contains the stable commit's files. Consumers cannot reliably reconstruct or publish the returned commit.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the selected channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot reports commit as repo.headCommit(channel), but obtains files from repo.headCommit("stable"). For any channel whose head differs from stable, the Snapshot describes one commit while containing another commit's file list.

findings.title: Honor the public limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=3)` still returns ten items because the implementation unconditionally sets `max_count = 10`. Callers cannot use the newly exposed limit contract.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: build(prefix, limit=2) still returns 10 entries because the loop uses a hard-coded max_count. The public signature promises caller-controlled result sizing, but its value is never applied.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=3)` still returns 10 entries because the body always assigns `max_count = 10`. The added parameter promises a caller-observable result limit but has no effect.

findings.title: Reject zero and negative values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts 0 and negative values. For example, charge("-1") now returns -100 cents rather than rejecting an invalid charge amount.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int('-1')` returns `-1`, so `charge('-1')` returns `-100`. The new public name promises positive input validation, but callers receive an invalid negative monetary amount instead.

findings.title: Validate positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts 0 and negative values. Consequently charge(-1) returns -100, so callers trusting the renamed contract can create negative charges.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame when applying mapped values
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the function made a copy before assigning values, so callers could retain and reuse the original DataFrame. Assigning through df now mutates that input; any caller holding it observes changed values even if it only intended to use the returned transformed frame.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame when applying mappings
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing df.copy() changes the function from returning an independent transformed DataFrame to modifying df in place. A caller that retains df for later use will observe its original values unexpectedly overwritten after calling apply_values.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed df.copy() means assignments now modify the DataFrame supplied by the caller. Previously callers could retain and reuse df unchanged while receiving a separately transformed result; after this change, the source data has its matching value cells overwritten.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int

findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` takes ownership of the `Vec<String>` and its returned value is discarded by the semicolon. The following `items.len()` therefore uses a moved value, causing Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Do not move items before calculating its length
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` consumes the `Vec<String>` expression. The subsequent `items.len()` therefore borrows a moved value and fails compilation with Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Avoid moving items before computing its length
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and returns the owned `Vec<String>`; because the returned value is discarded by the statement, `items` is moved and dropped. The subsequent `items.len()` borrows a moved value, producing Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the returned base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `Changeset.fromRevision` promises the revision against which `changedPaths` was computed and which consumers replay onto. This now returns paths computed from `latest` while declaring the pinned-tag revision as the base; when those resolve differently, replay uses a mismatched changeset and can omit or apply incorrect paths.

findings.title: Compute paths from the declared base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `fromRevision` remains the revision resolved from `pinnedTag`, but `changedPaths` is now computed from `latest`. When those tags differ, paths changed between the pinned revision and latest are omitted while consumers replay the changeset against the pinned revision, violating the exported Changeset contract.

findings.title: Read changed paths from the pinned revision
findings.whyItBreaks: Changeset.fromRevision remains the resolved pinned tag, while changedPaths is computed from "latest". Consumers replay paths on top of fromRevision, so this can select paths that do not correspond to the revision they replay.

findings.whyItBreaks: `load_settings()` returns `None` for a nonexistent path, and removing the fallback makes `settings["workers"]` raise `TypeError`. Previously this startup path returned the default worker count of 1.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-settings fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (line 7). With the fallback removed, startup evaluates settings["workers"] on None and raises TypeError instead of starting with the prior one-worker default.

findings.title: Restore fallback for a missing settings file
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (line 7); startup now immediately subscripts that None, raising TypeError instead of retaining the prior default worker configuration.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error then returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a declined/failed payment from a successful charge and can proceed as if payment completed.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge logs it and returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a failed charge from a successful one and may mark an unpaid transaction as paid.

findings.title: Propagate failed gateway submissions
findings.whyItBreaks: A gateway failure is logged but Charge returns nil, so callers cannot distinguish a declined/failed payment from a completed charge and may proceed as if payment succeeded.

findings.title: Include tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants requesting the same setting name now share `settings:<name>`. After tenant A caches `theme`, tenant B receives A's value at the cache-hit branch instead of calling `store.fetch(tenantB, "theme")`.

findings.title: Preserve tenant-scoped invalidation
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported API no longer accepts the existing `(tenantId, name)` contract. TypeScript consumers fail to compile; JavaScript consumers passing both arguments silently use the tenant ID as `name`, deleting `settings:<tenantId>` and leaving the intended setting cached.

findings.title: Keep tenantId in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key is now derived only from name. After tenant A fetches "theme", a fetch for tenant B with the same name returns tenant A's cached value at line 14 and never calls the tenant-scoped store fetch at line 15.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the settings cache key

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two callers can both read remaining=1 before either awaited save resumes. Both save 0, both return true, and two units are successfully reserved despite only one being available. Before this change reserve had no await, so the first call updated stock before another call could observe it.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Inventory API or release it as breaking
findings.whyItBreaks: Inventory is exported, but existing consumers using new Inventory() now construct an instance with no store at runtime and fail when reserve calls save. TypeScript consumers also receive Promise<boolean> instead of boolean; un-awaited boolean checks treat the Promise as truthy, so out-of-stock reservations can be accepted.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await yields before stock is updated. With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls both read remaining=1, both save 0, both return true, and only one unit is recorded as removed. Callers can fulfill two reservations for a single item.

findings.title: Preserve the exported Inventory API contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers cannot construct Inventory without a Store, and existing JavaScript callers treating reserve's boolean result as a condition now receive a truthy Promise. For example, an out-of-stock reserve formerly returned false but now makes `if (inventory.reserve(sku))` proceed.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two concurrent calls both read remaining=1 before either await completes, both save 0, both set stock to 0, and both return true. This permits two successful reservations for one unit.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but `retry` still multiplies it by 1,000 before passing it to its millisecond-based `sleep` helper. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) rather than 1 second; capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms (8h20m) rather than 30 seconds.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff()` now returns milliseconds, as reflected by the updated poll caller, but `retry()` still multiplies it by 1,000. Its first retry therefore sleeps 1,000,000 ms (16.7 minutes) instead of 1,000 ms, and capped retries sleep 30,000,000 ms (8.3 hours).

findings.title: Remove retry's stale seconds-to-milliseconds conversion
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff` now returns milliseconds, and polling was updated accordingly. `retry` still calls `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, so its first retry waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16m40s) instead of 1,000 ms; the capped delay becomes about 8h20m instead of 30s.

findings.title: Propagate the final file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close return value is ignored. When Flush succeeds but the final Close fails, Save now returns nil although the write was not successfully finalized; before this change, that Close error was returned to the caller.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is ignored. Previously a successful Flush returned f.Close()'s error, so callers could detect a failed final close; now Save returns nil after a successful flush even if close fails.

findings.title: Propagate the file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. After a successful Flush, a close-time write/finalization error is now reported as nil, whereas the previous implementation returned that error to Save callers.

findings.title: Include the page end position when collecting rows
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open end, but range(start, end - 1) excludes both end and the last valid index. A one-row page returns no rows; larger pages omit their final row, so render_page and summarize silently lose data.

findings.title: Include each page's endpoint row
findings.whyItBreaks: The computed bounds are half-open [start, end), but range(start, end - 1) excludes index end - 1. Every rendered page drops its final row; with page_size=1, summarize produces empty pages.

findings.title: Include the page end position when collecting rows
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns an exclusive end, but range(start, end - 1) excludes both end - 1 and end. For example, three rows with page_size=2 render page 0 as only row 1 and page 1 as empty, dropping rows 2 and 3 from summarize output.

findings.title: Restore the cache-expiration comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: For a normal positive TTL, a freshly stored entry has age < ttlMs and is now deleted as a miss; once it is older than the TTL, it is returned as a stale hit.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next item into the current index, but forEach then advances its index. For two adjacent done jobs, the second remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve pruneDone's non-mutating return behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior filter implementation returned a new array and left the caller's jobs array intact. This exported function now removes elements from the caller-owned array, which is an observable upgrade-breaking API behavior change.

findings.title: Restore the non-expired cache predicate
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age 0, so it fails `0 > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Entries instead become readable only after expiry and are never removed on reads.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: `forEach` advances its index after `splice`; when two adjacent jobs are done, removing the first shifts the second into the already-visited index, leaving that completed job in the returned queue.

findings.title: Restore the non-expired cache-hit condition
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age near zero, so `age > ttlMs` is false and `get` deletes it instead of returning it. Conversely, entries older than the TTL are returned as cache hits.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next item into the current index, but `forEach` advances to the next index. For `[doneA, doneB]`, `doneA` is removed and `doneB` is skipped, so it remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve pruneDone's non-mutating return contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior `filter` implementation returned a new array and left the caller's `jobs` array intact. This change splices and returns the same input array, breaking existing callers that retain the original queue for retry, logging, or comparison.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average result
findings.whyItBreaks: For [], total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN instead of the previous numeric fallback 0. Consumers performing arithmetic, serialization, or display receive an invalid numeric result.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. Calling busiest now changes the caller's input order, whereas the prior implementation sorted a copy; later processing that relies on original row order observes changed data.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average value
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, reduce returns 0 and division by rows.length produces NaN. The prior implementation returned 0, so consumers now receive a non-numeric statistic for a valid empty dataset.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller’s rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. Previously busiest sorted a copy, so callers could reuse their input ordering; this change silently reorders that input while selecting the busiest row.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-set average
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN instead of the prior numeric sentinel 0. Consumers of the exported number can no longer treat an empty dataset as a zero average.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's rows in place
findings.whyItBreaks: busiest previously sorted a copy. It now reorders the supplied rows array, so callers that retain the array observe their input order changed merely by asking for the busiest row.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending score sorting
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator compares numeric scores as strings. For scores [100, 9, 80], reversal produces [9, 80, 100], so topPlayers(..., 1) uses 9 as the cutoff and returns the first input player instead of the highest-scoring player.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending score comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders scores as strings. For input scores [2, 10, 9] with n=2, rankScores returns [9, 2, 10], making the cutoff 2; topPlayers then returns the first two input players (2 and 10), omitting the player with score 9.

findings.title: Restore numeric ordering for score ranking
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator converts numbers to strings. For players ordered [{score: 2}, {score: 10}] with n=1, rankScores produces [2, 10], making the cutoff 2; topPlayers then returns the first 2-point player instead of the 10-point player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can return on the first mismatched character, exposing how much of an attacker-supplied HMAC matches the expected signature. An attacker able to repeatedly measure verification time can recover a valid signature and cause handle() to invoke processor() for an unauthenticated payload.

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using string equality can return after the first differing character, making verification time depend on how much of an attacker-supplied signature matches the expected HMAC. The result gates execution of processor(payload), so repeated requests can expose a timing oracle for forging a valid signature.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` short-circuits on the first differing character. Since `handle` exposes an authentication success/failure decision, an attacker can repeatedly measure responses to infer matching HMAC prefix characters. The prior `hmac.compare_digest` avoided this timing oracle.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance mutations in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the transaction exits at line 23. If either subsequent balance update raises, transfer returns an error after permanently recording a ledger transfer whose balances were not fully applied.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after `_record_ledger`. If either balance update then fails, or the process stops between the committed ledger insert and the balance updates, a transfer is recorded without matching balance changes; failure during the second update can also leave only the debit applied. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the context exits at line 23. If either balance UPDATE then fails, the ledger records a completed transfer while one or neither account balance changes; if the second UPDATE fails, the sender is debited without crediting the recipient. The base revision made all three writes atomic.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving billing dates
findings.whyItBreaks: For instants near midnight UTC, this returns a different billing-day key on non-UTC hosts. For example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z is billed as 2025-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles, whereas the previous implementation consistently returned 2026-01-01. This can split the same billing period across deployments or move charges into the prior day.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: This changes the established API behavior from UTC calendar dates to the runtime's local timezone. For example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z produced 2026-01-01 before, but produces 2025-12-31 on a host in America/Los_Angeles. Billing-day keys and sameBillingDay comparisons consequently vary by deployment timezone.

findings.title: Keep billing-day keys in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation deliberately used UTC getters. The new local-time getters classify the same instant differently by process timezone; for example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes billing day 2025-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles. This changes billing keys and sameBillingDay results across deployment regions.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After fetching and caching `tenantA/accountX`, a request for `tenantB/accountX` hits the same `accountX` key at line 15 and returns tenantA's Profile without calling fetchProfile. This returns incorrect tenant data and can expose one tenant's profile to another.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Profiles are fetched using both tenant and account, and Profile includes a tenant field. After tenant A/account X is cached, a request for tenant B/account X returns A's profile without calling fetchProfile.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants with the same account value now share one memo entry. After tenant A loads account X, tenant B's request for account X returns tenant A's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile, exposing incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. `loadAll` consequently returns partial-looking successful data instead of reporting a missing requested key.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `missing: <key>`, but now returns the valid string value `""`. Callers, including `loadAll`, cannot distinguish absent data from an intentionally stored empty string and will continue with silently corrupted results.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is also a valid stored value. Consumers, including loadAll, can no longer distinguish absent data from intentionally empty data and may process the fallback as real content.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing retry configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported interface removes `timeoutMs` and adds required `retries`. Existing TypeScript consumers constructing the previously valid `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` config no longer compile. Untyped consumers calling `retry` with that old object get `config.timeout === undefined`; line 8 computes a `NaN` deadline, so `Date.now() > deadline` at line 10 is always false and the timeout is silently disabled.

findings.title: Make retryBackground actually execute in the background
findings.whyItBreaks: `retryBackground` is an exported API whose name promises background execution, but it invokes `fn()` synchronously on line 25 and does not return until an attempt succeeds, the deadline expires, or retries are exhausted. Callers using it to keep foreground work non-blocking will still be blocked by the callback and retry loop.

findings.title: Expose terminal retry failure to retryBackground callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from `fn` is caught and, after the final attempt or deadline, the exported function returns `void` exactly as it does on success. Its callers therefore cannot distinguish successful work from work that failed on every attempt and may proceed as though the background operation completed.

findings.title: Expose exhaustion failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from fn is discarded, and exhausting retries returns normally with void—the same observable result as success. As an exported API, this forces callers to treat permanent failure as success and can let them continue after failed work.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing retry Config callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and consumed by retry. Existing callers that supply { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } now fail TypeScript checking because retries and timeout are required. JavaScript callers instead compute Date.now() + undefined, producing NaN; the deadline guard never fires, so their configured timeout is silently ignored.

findings.title: Propagate failure after background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported retryBackground catches every exception and returns void after the final failed attempt. Its caller cannot distinguish an exhausted failure from a successful invocation, so it can continue, persist state, or report success after fn never completed.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before measuring length
findings.whyItBreaks: The public type promises that `value` may be a number, but the changed body reads `value.length`. TypeScript rejects this access for `string | number`; if emitted without type checking, `Field({ value: 42 })` renders `len=undefined` rather than a numeric-length label.

findings.title: Handle number values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now publicly accepts `number`, but `number` has no `length` property. This produces a TypeScript error and makes the newly advertised numeric usage unusable.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly accepts number values, but number has no length property. TypeScript rejects this access, and JavaScript callers passing a number receive "len=undefined" instead of a meaningful label.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The shared git wrapper now uses spawnSync's default 1 MiB maxBuffer. runGithub uses it to capture the full patch at line 140; a PR diff exceeding that size causes spawnSync to terminate with ENOBUFS/status null, so the review fails rather than reviewing the PR. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these diffs.

findings.title: Restore a buffer limit for Git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB stdout/stderr limit. A PR whose textual `git diff` exceeds that limit is terminated; the status check throws, and runGithub reports the review as failed instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for Git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. runGithub reads the complete PR patch through this helper at line 140, so a diff exceeding 1 MiB terminates with a buffer error before any review is posted; the previous 64 MiB limit supported such reviews.

findings.title: Pass the merge base that matches the generated patch
findings.whyItBreaks: patch and changedFiles are computed from mergeBase..headSha (lines 140-141), but the review bundle now declares baseSha as the target branch tip. When the target branch has advanced since the PR branch diverged, the stated base..head range includes target-only commits absent from the supplied patch and file list, so review consumers can inspect and report on a different range than the one being reviewed.

findings.title: Restore the explicit read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `-s read-only`, `runCodex` loads the local Codex configuration and no longer constrains model-generated shell commands. A workspace-write policy can therefore let the review agent modify `opts.repoPath`, the repository it is meant to inspect.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for reviewer execution
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` lets the Codex subprocess use its configured/default sandbox while running against `opts.repoPath`. Review prompts and reviewed content can then cause filesystem mutations in the checkout, violating the reviewer's read-only safety boundary and risking unintended source changes or deletion.

findings.title: Keep Codex execution in the read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `-s read-only`, the spawned `codex exec` loads its ambient configuration and may use a writable sandbox. This helper runs with `cwd: opts.repoPath`, so a prompt or repository-controlled instruction can cause the review subprocess to alter the repository rather than merely inspect it.

findings.title: Compare the PR from its merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA is the current base tip, not necessarily the point where the PR branch diverged. For a long-lived PR with base-only commits after divergence, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes inverse changes for those base-only commits, so unrelated files are supplied to the reviewer and may receive review findings.

findings.title: Build the review surface from the configured PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA is set and the checkout is not that commit (for example, a merge-ref checkout), the bundle declares and posts results for PR_HEAD_SHA but analyzes `HEAD`. The generated patch and changed-path set can therefore describe a different commit than the review and check run target.

findings.title: Build review context from the PR head's merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA may be the current target-branch tip rather than an ancestor of the PR head. Diffing it directly against HEAD includes target-only commits as apparent PR changes. These lines also ignore PR_HEAD_SHA, so an Action checkout at a merge commit or another ref sends a patch/file list for HEAD while posting the review against headSha.

findings.title: Restore merge-base selection for the PR diff
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current base-branch tip and the PR branch diverged earlier, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes the base branch's post-divergence changes as reversions as well as the PR changes. The review bundle and changed-file set therefore contain files the PR did not modify, allowing false findings and invalid inline-comment eligibility. The previous code correctly derived the common ancestor before diffing.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt input during replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets `$&`, `$'`, `$`` and `$$` in a string replacement. Bundle data includes the untrusted raw patch, and JSON.stringify does not escape `$`; consequently a patch containing `$&` is delivered to Codex as `{{PATCH}}` instead of its original text. `$'` and `$`` can additionally duplicate portions of the prompt, so reviews may be performed against a corrupted bundle or diff.

findings.title: Keep prompt payloads literal during placeholder substitution
findings.whyItBreaks: String replacement arguments interpret `$&`, `$`` and `$'` specially. A patch, bundle field, or candidate finding containing one of these sequences is no longer inserted literally: for example, a diff containing `$&` at line 33 leaves `{{PATCH}}` in the critic prompt instead of the diff. This makes reviews omit or corrupt user-supplied context before it reaches runCodex.

findings.title: Preserve dollar sequences when expanding the patch placeholder
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets $& and related sequences in a string replacement. A reviewed patch containing, for example, "$&" is sent to the critic with "{{PATCH}}" substituted into its source instead of the original text, so the critic can review corrupted diff content.

findings.title: Bind the fallback review to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The review result is computed from headSha (lines 141-145), but omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the fallback review to the PR's most recent commit. If the PR is updated while review() runs and the first POST fails (for example due to invalid inline comments), a REQUEST_CHANGES result for the old diff is submitted against the new head.

findings.title: Keep fallback review bound to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial review creation fails (for example, because an inline comment is rejected), the fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then applies the review to the PR's current head. If a new commit is pushed after this run computed its result for headSha, the fallback can post stale findings or REQUEST_CHANGES against that newer, unreviewed commit. The primary path and check run both remain explicitly bound to headSha.

findings.title: Keep fallback review pinned to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial request fails (for example, due to an invalid inline comment), this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. If the PR is updated after headSha is captured and reviewed but before this fallback posts, Needlefish's pass or request-changes review is recorded against the newer, unreviewed commit.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid review output no longer produces an error: for example, an invalid severity and missing location are converted into a P1 bug at file "" and line 0. normalizeReview then returns success, so callers cannot distinguish malformed model output from a real finding.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict-mode parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the optional strict argument is a source-compatible API break for TypeScript consumers that call normalizeReview(raw, false). JavaScript callers also lose the documented behavior of dropping malformed findings; they now receive fabricated default findings instead.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid required fields now lose their validation error and are returned as real findings: for example, a missing file and lineStart become file="" and lineStart=0. normalizeReview then returns this non-addressable finding to its callers rather than signaling malformed review output.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict-mode parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported second parameter is an upgrade break: existing TypeScript callers of normalizeReview(raw, false) no longer type-check. JavaScript callers also lose the documented lenient behavior of dropping malformed findings and instead receive fabricated default findings.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid required data no longer reaches the validation error path. For example, an invalid severity becomes P1, an invalid category becomes bug, and missing file/line data becomes an empty path and line 0. normalizeReview now returns those fabricated findings as normal results, so downstream consumers cannot distinguish malformed model output from a real P1 finding.

findings.title: Keep the repository selector for manual PR resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this runs before the Checkout PR head step. Without -R "$REPO", gh pr view must infer a repository from a local git remote, but no checkout exists yet. The manually requested PR refs therefore cannot be resolved and the review job stops before checkout.

findings.title: Keep the explicit repository when resolving dispatched PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before actions/checkout. Removing -R leaves gh pr view with no repository source on a clean self-hosted runner; it cannot resolve the requested PR's head/base. The resulting empty/invalid outputs make checkout fail or select a non-PR ref.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and this branch runs before any checkout. Without -R "$REPO" (or GH_REPO), gh pr view must infer a repository from the runner's current Git remote, which is not guaranteed to exist in an un-checked-out Actions workspace. The refs step then fails, preventing the manual review workflow from running.

findings.title: Reject malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or invalid review fields are converted to empty strings/arrays instead of raising the prior malformed-output error. Consumers therefore cannot distinguish a failed or truncated reviewer response from a legitimate review with no findings or blocking risks.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs previously rejected as malformed (including a non-object or missing findings/checked/residual_risks) now produce an empty RawReview. Callers cannot distinguish failed or truncated reviewer output from a legitimate no-findings review, so they may treat an invalid response as a successful PASS-like result.

findings.title: Reject malformed review payloads instead of defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported normalizer now maps a missing or malformed summary/findings/checked/residual_risks field to empty values. Callers can no longer distinguish an invalid reviewer response from a legitimate no-findings review, so malformed output may be accepted and reported as an empty review.

findings.title: Restore PR-head resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so this falls back to github.ref—the branch/ref selected to run the workflow, not the PR identified by pr_number. The workflow consequently installs and executes the reviewer from that unrelated ref rather than the requested PR head. The removed resolver specifically queried pr_number for head/base SHAs on this path.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request payload. Consequently the checkout falls back to the workflow ref, the base fetch falls back to main, and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are empty instead of referring to the requested pr_number. Manual reviews therefore run with the wrong source/revision data (and cannot correctly review PRs targeting non-main branches).

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so both variables evaluate to empty strings. The manually supplied pr_number is therefore reviewed without its base/head SHAs; checkout also uses github.ref rather than the requested PR head. The removed Resolve PR refs step previously queried these exact values with `gh pr view` for this path.

findings.title: Restore the git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` obtains the complete patch with `git diff` at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses its 1 MiB default; larger diffs terminate with a buffer error and `git()` throws, so the local reviewer cannot review repositories with diffs that previously fit the explicit 64 MiB limit.

findings.title: Restore a buffer large enough for review patches
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. runLocal captures the complete `git diff` into `patch`; a patch exceeding that limit makes spawnSync fail and this wrapper throws, preventing review of otherwise valid large changes. The previous 64 MiB limit supported those inputs.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for review diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` captures the complete `git diff` output at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, Node's `spawnSync` default is 1 MiB; a diff larger than that terminates with `ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER`, so local review fails before submitting the bundle. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these diffs.

findings.title: Keep review failures as failed checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or publishing the review throws, this posts conclusion=neutral even though the message says the review did not pass. GitHub treats neutral required checks as non-failing, so a PR can remain mergeable despite Needlefish being unable to perform its review.

findings.title: Report review execution errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, the error path still says the PR did not pass, but posts a neutral check conclusion. GitHub treats neutral as non-failing for required-check evaluation, so a branch requiring the Needlefish check can permit merge despite no review result being produced.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews as failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or review posting throws, this catch path reports the Needlefish check as neutral. GitHub accepts neutral as a successful required status check, so a repository requiring the Needlefish check can permit merging despite the review having errored. The prior implementation reported failure.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer executable outside the PR checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The job checks out the PR head at lines 43-47, then installs and executes its package and src/cli.ts. An internal PR can change that CLI or package lifecycle scripts to forge its review result or use the GH_TOKEN granted pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions. The removed second checkout previously ensured the reviewer came from trusted main.

findings.title: Run a reviewer that exists in this checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: Both base and head trees contain only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json: there is no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, node_modules/.bin/tsx, or src/cli.ts. The new install and execution steps therefore cannot run the review workflow. The removed trusted checkout was the only source of these files.

findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out revision contains only this workflow and .needlefish/answers.json; it has neither src/cli.ts nor a committed dependency manifest. This command therefore cannot invoke the reviewer, so every review job fails instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow checks out the PR head at lines 43-47, installs its dependencies at line 51, and executes its src/cli.ts here with a GH_TOKEN that can write pull requests and checks. Any same-repository PR can alter the reviewer or install lifecycle code to suppress findings or execute privileged actions; the job condition explicitly permits those PRs.

The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the reviewer package
findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out repository contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, src/, or CLI. Consequently, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile fails before the review step, so every review job is unusable.

findings.title: Do not execute the reviewer from the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is checked out at the workspace root and this command executes its src/cli.ts with a GITHUB_TOKEN that has pull-requests: write and checks: write. A same-repository PR can supply a modified reviewer that suppresses or fabricates review results, defeating the workflow's review gate; the prior workflow deliberately executed the separately checked-out main branch tool instead.

The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Preserve severity normalization before validation
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw output and passes each finding to normalizeFinding. Previously inputs such as "p1" or " P2 " were normalized to P1/P2; this exact-match check rejects them and assigns P3 instead, silently understating valid finding severity.

findings.title: Restore severity canonicalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external JSON and passes each finding here. A previously accepted severity such as " p2 " or "p0" now fails the exact includes check and is silently emitted as P3, rather than being canonicalized to P2/P0. This regresses the exported normalizer's established behavior and can make real findings appear less severe.

findings.title: Preserve severity canonicalization before validation
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw review JSON and passes each finding here. A valid producer value such as " p0 " or "p2" was previously canonicalized to P0/P2; it is now rejected by the exact-match check and emitted as P3, silently downgrading the finding.

findings.title: Remove GitHub credentials from the Codex subprocess environment
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit environment scrub makes the spawned `codex exec` process inherit `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. `prompt` is supplied to this exported runner, and Codex can invoke shell commands; a malicious or compromised prompt/repository can read these credentials and send them externally.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit environment allowlist makes spawnSync inherit process.env. Thus GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN that were deliberately removed before are available to the Codex process and any commands it invokes while inspecting an arbitrary repository. A malicious repository instruction or prompt-injected tool call can read and exfiltrate those credentials despite the read-only filesystem sandbox.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env object, spawnSync inherits process.env. Thus GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN become available to Codex while it processes repository-controlled prompt/diff content; those credentials can authenticate GitHub API or git operations and were previously deliberately withheld.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running the PR checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the repository-identity condition allows pull_request events from forks to run this job. The workflow checks out the fork-controlled SHA and then executes both its dependency installation and src/cli.ts on a self-hosted runner, giving a fork author arbitrary code execution in that runner's environment.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job-level repository check makes this pull_request workflow run for forked PRs. It checks out the fork's exact head SHA, installs its dependency graph, and executes its src/cli.ts on a self-hosted runner. A fork author can therefore run arbitrary code in that runner environment.

findings.title: Restore the fork trust boundary before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted job-level condition previously excluded fork PRs. Now any fork can supply the checked-out commit, dependency metadata, and src/cli.ts, all of which are executed by pnpm install and tsx on the self-hosted runner. This gives external contributors arbitrary code execution in the trusted runner environment.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration runner settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, setting either NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 produced an immediate next timeout stage. This change treats 0 as invalid and silently substitutes 5000 ms or 2000 ms, so existing configurations that intentionally disable the grace/give-up delay gain an unexpected delay after upgrade.

findings.title: Preserve zero as a valid runner timing value
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, setting either NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 was accepted and produced an immediate next timeout action. This change silently substitutes the 5000 ms or 2000 ms fallback instead, so existing deployments that intentionally require immediate SIGKILL or immediate completion after SIGKILL gain an unexpected delay.

findings.title: Preserve explicit zero-duration configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 were accepted and passed to setTimeout, producing immediate escalation/completion. The new > 0 guard rejects those explicit settings and silently substitutes 5000ms or 2000ms, changing existing deployments' timeout behavior after upgrade.

findings.title: Restore coverage for unmapped large-PR files
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapped hotspots are deep-reviewed. Removing the tail-coverage hotspot means files omitted by the mapper, or assigned to a hotspot beyond the six-item cap, receive no deep review; the critic receives only patch statistics and can return a clean result despite an unreviewed changed file.

findings.title: Propagate deep-review residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: Residual risks emitted by successful deep reviews are replaced with an empty array before the critic sees them. In particular, a blocking uncertainty found by a deep pass is no longer available to the critic or final verdict, so an incomplete review can be returned without its blocker.

findings.title: Restore coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews select at most six mapper hotspots, but no longer create a tail hotspot for changed files omitted by those selections. A mapper result with more than six hotspots, or one that does not assign every changed file, now leaves those files entirely unreviewed and can return a passing review despite defects in them.

findings.title: Keep deep-review failures as blocking results
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed deep-review invocation now rejects reviewLarge immediately. Previously the failure was recorded as a blocking residual risk and the remaining hotspots were reviewed, so callers received a ReviewResult that clearly could not pass. One transient worker failure now produces no review result at all.

findings.title: Forward deep-review residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Successful deep passes can return residual risks, including blocks=true, but the merged candidate now replaces all of them with an empty array. The critic and final verdict therefore cannot distinguish an unresolved blocking risk from a clean deep review, allowing a pass to be emitted without the required uncertainty signal.

findings.title: Deep-review changed files outside the first six hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: For a large PR whose map contains more than six distinct hotspots, slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) excludes the remaining files and the removed tail-coverage pass no longer schedules them for deep review. The final critic receives only the selected review results, so a changed file can be omitted from review entirely.

findings.title: Retain residual risks from each deep review
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep review's residual_risks, including blocks:true uncertainty, is now replaced with an empty array before the critic runs. The critic and final verdict therefore cannot distinguish a fully reviewed large PR from one with an explicitly unresolved deep-review risk, and can emit a non-blocking result.

findings.title: Keep per-hotspot failure isolation
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed runCodex call for any one hotspot now rejects reviewLarge and discards all prior deep-review results. Previously the failure was represented as a blocking residual risk and the caller still received a ReviewResult describing the incomplete review.

findings.title: Preserve focus when running the large-review pipeline
findings.whyItBreaks: For patches over the large-review threshold, `review()` routes to `reviewLarge()`, which now omits `bundle.focus` from the map prompt and no longer substitutes `{{FOCUS}}` in each deep prompt. A caller-provided focus therefore works for small reviews but is ignored for large ones, causing the highest-risk review path to miss the requested area.

findings.title: Preserve focus and depth in large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() selects reviewLarge() for a patch over the size threshold, mapBundle no longer includes bundle.focus or bundle.deep. The subsequent deep-review prompt also no longer substitutes bundle.focus. Consequently, a caller-requested review focus/depth is ignored only for large patches, causing hotspot selection and deep review to cover a different scope than requested.

findings.title: Forward focus into large-review deep passes
findings.whyItBreaks: When isLarge routes a focus-bearing Bundle here, the removed {{FOCUS}} substitution means every deep prompt retains the literal placeholder instead of the requested focus. The mapping input also no longer contains focus, so large reviews lose this caller directive entirely, while small reviews still serialize it in the full bundle.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations whose remaining milliseconds round to 60 seconds, such as 119500ms, this renders `1m 60s` rather than `2m 0s`. The prior total-second rounding correctly carried the overflow.

findings.title: Normalize seconds that round to a full minute
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, minutes is 1 while the remainder rounds to 60 seconds, so rendered stats show `1m 60s` instead of normalized `2m 0s`. The previous total-second calculation carried this rounding into minutes.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500 ms, minutes is 1 and seconds rounds to 60, so rendered review statistics say "1m 60s" instead of the previous correctly rounded "2m 0s".

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` return 0, while both its exported name and thrown-error contract promise a positive integer. Public callers can now receive a value outside the declared result domain.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: For input "0", Number.isInteger(parsed) is true and parsed < 0 is false, so this exported function returns 0 even though its name and thrown-error contract promise a positive integer.

findings.title: Reject zero to preserve the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns `0`, although its exported name and unchanged error contract promise a positive integer. Callers can consequently accept an invalid zero value wherever this parser is used.
